theory.title: BGP: Routing Between Networks
theory.recap: You know how routing tables direct packets within a single network using longest-prefix matching. But the internet is not one network - it is tens of thousands of independent networks (Autonomous Systems) that must agree on how to route between each other.
theory.plainObjective: Navigate from AS1 through AS2 to reach the destination in AS3. Each AS node has a BGP table showing which neighbor leads toward the destination prefix. Apply longest-prefix matching at each AS node.
theory.summary: BGP is the glue that holds the internet together. Every packet crossing ISP boundaries uses BGP routing decisions. Without BGP, the internet would fragment into isolated islands. Every major internet outage (Facebook 2021, AWS 2021) traces back to a BGP misconfiguration.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Autonomous Systems
bodyParagraphs.text:
An Autonomous System (AS) is a network under single administrative control - an ISP, university, or cloud provider. Each AS has a globally unique AS number (ASN):
  • AS 15169 - Google
  • AS 16509 - Amazon AWS
  • AS 32934 - Meta

bodyParagraphs.heading: BGP peering
bodyParagraphs.text: Two AS operators configure a BGP session between their routers (BGP peers). They exchange routing information: "I can reach 203.0.113.0/24 via my network." Routes propagate hop by hop until every AS knows a path to every prefix.

bodyParagraphs.heading: AS path
bodyParagraphs.text: BGP advertises not just the prefix but the full list of ASes to reach it. An AS path of 64500 64501 64502 means the packet traverses three ASes. Longer AS paths are less preferred.

bodyParagraphs.heading: BGP tables use CIDR, just like IP routing
bodyParagraphs.text: BGP tables are routing tables with CIDR prefixes - the same longest-prefix match algorithm applies. The difference: entries come from BGP peers rather than local configuration.

theory.mission:
You carry a packet from AS1 (srcIP: 203.0.113.5) destined for 198.51.100.10 in AS3.

Each AS node has a BGP table. Apply longest-prefix matching at each hop. Some exits lead to the wrong AS - the BGP table will tell you which exit is correct.

termIntroductions.headline: BGP
termIntroductions.body: Border Gateway Protocol is how autonomous systems on the internet exchange routing information. Every ISP, cloud provider, and large organization has an ASN. BGP sessions between peers propagate reachability: 'I can reach 198.51.100.0/24'. Without BGP, inter-AS routing would be impossible.

termIntroductions.headline: Autonomous System
termIntroductions.body: AS1 (ASN 64500) is your source network. Each AS runs its own internal routing (OSPF or IS-IS) and connects to other ASes via BGP. The BGP table here shows which peer AS to send packets toward for each destination prefix. 198.51.100.0/24 lives in AS3.

termIntroductions.headline: AS Path
termIntroductions.body: AS2 learned that 198.51.100.0/24 is reachable via peer AS3 (one hop). The alternative is AS5 which has no route to that prefix. BGP prefers shorter AS paths - this is why packets take efficient routes across the internet rather than wandering aimlessly.
